title: Invoice Export
tagline: Bookkeepers get every invoice out of Fieldnote in one click, in their tool's format.

summary.headline: Month end costs each bookkeeper about three hours of copying. One Export button, in their tool's format, ends it.
paragraphs: Every month our customers' bookkeepers rebuild a spreadsheet from Fieldnote by hand and download PDFs one at a time. Totals drift, and in the Americas the month itself ends on the wrong day because our dates are in UTC.

The fix is one export: the right month in the account's time zone, a CSV for QuickBooks, Xero or FreeAgent, every PDF in one zip, a record of who took what, and a monthly email on the day the owner closes the books.
Eight tickets in three waves. The first wave is built and verified; the second is building now.

problems.title: Bookkeepers copy every invoice into a spreadsheet by hand
problems.asked: Make it one button. My bookkeeper should never need to log in.
problems.problem: There is no export. Each month a bookkeeper opens every invoice, types its number, client and total into a sheet, then imports that sheet into their accounting tool.
problems.why: It takes about three hours per account each month, and typing errors make the books disagree with Fieldnote. It is the top request in support.

found.text: 41 support tickets in September asked for an export, more than any other request.
Five of five bookkeepers interviewed rebuild the sheet by hand; the median takes three hours.
QuickBooks, Xero and FreeAgent each want different column names and date formats.
The invoice list already loads every field an export needs.

solution.summary: Add one Export button to the invoice list. It opens a short dialog: pick the tool, the month, and whether to include PDFs. The file arrives in that tool's own format.
points: Three presets, one per accounting tool, each a column map and a date format.
The dialog remembers the last choice, so the second export is one click.
Exports run as a background job, so a large month never times out.
not_doing: A direct sync with each accounting tool. Files cover every customer we have; syncs can come later.
A custom column builder. Three presets cover all 41 requests.
solution.reference: Stripe's invoice export works this way: one button, a format picker, the file emailed when ready. FreshBooks offers the same three accounting presets.

problems.title: PDFs download one at a time, four seconds each
problems.problem: Each invoice PDF is drawn on the web server when someone clicks it. A month of 200 invoices means 200 clicks and about 13 minutes of waiting.
problems.why: Bookkeepers need every PDF for their records. Drawing on the web server also slows the app for everyone during month end.

found.text: A PDF takes 3.8 to 4.4 seconds to draw, measured on 50 invoices.
The same invoice is redrawn every time, even when nothing changed.
App response time doubles on the first two days of each month.

solution.summary: Draw PDFs in a worker, eight at a time, and keep each one until its invoice changes. An export bundles them into one zip.
points: A cache keyed by invoice id and version, so a PDF is drawn once.
The zip streams as it fills, so the first bytes arrive at once.
not_doing: A new PDF design. The layout stays exactly as it is.
solution.reference: Shopify draws order PDFs in background workers and caches them by order version.

visuals.label: Diagram
visuals.caption: The export job hands PDFs to a worker and a cache.

outcome: 200 PDFs arrive in one zip in under 60 seconds.
The app stays as fast on the first of the month as on any other day.

problems.title: Month ends land on the wrong day in the Americas
problems.problem: Date filters use UTC. An invoice sent at 7 pm in Los Angeles on 31 October counts as November.
problems.why: The export would carry the same error into the books, so totals per month would never match the bank.

found.text: The range query compares created_at with UTC midnight.
1 in 9 October invoices for US accounts fell in the wrong month.
found.evidence: Query on a copy of October data, 3 Nov

solution.summary: Read each account's time zone and build month boundaries in it before querying.
points: Every export, and the invoice list filter, use the same boundary function.
solution.reference: Stripe reports use the account's time zone for every date boundary.

outcome: An invoice belongs to the month its account saw it in.

problems.title: Nobody can see who took which invoices out
problems.problem: Downloads leave no record. An owner cannot tell whether last month was exported, or by whom.
problems.why: Two bookkeepers sometimes import the same month twice, which doubles revenue in the books.

found.text: Two accounts reported a doubled month in October.

solution.summary: Store each export as a row: who, when, which range, which format, and the file. Show them on an Export history page.
not_doing: Blocking a repeat export. We show it was done; the person decides.

outcome: An owner sees every export of the last year, with who ran it and the file.

problems.title: The monthly file should arrive on the owner's close day
problems.asked: The monthly email has to land on the day they close the month, not ours.
problems.problem: Owners want the export to send itself each month. Each closes the books on a different day.
problems.why: A file on the wrong day is stale or early, so the bookkeeper exports by hand anyway.

found.text: Owners named 1st, 3rd, 5th and last working day as their close day.

solution.summary: A setting for the close day. On that day an email goes to the bookkeeper with a link that expires after seven days.
solution.reference: Xero's scheduled reports let the owner pick the day and the recipients.

outcome: The bookkeeper gets last month's file on the owner's close day without logging in.

plan.goal: Ship one Export that is right to the cent, in every customer's time zone, with a record and a monthly send.

verification.strategy: Each ticket proves itself before its commit lands: tests for logic, a measured number for speed, a browser walk for screens. A Fable agent reviews every pull request. At the end an Opus agent runs one export end to end on a fresh local copy with all four pull requests, using a made up account in Los Angeles.
